blindSummary:
This country carries serious risk for trans visitors — the least hostile in its region, but not safe. In 2007 a penal-code provision criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" (up to 1 year in jail); within two weeks at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops and taxis, three were beaten (one into unconsciousness), and heads were shaved as punishment. An international human-rights organisation's 2012 report documented police violence against trans women under this law.

However, in February 2022 the constitutional court struck down that provision as unconstitutional — the only country in its region to repeal its cross-dressing statute. The repeal has teeth: a cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut won 4,000 units of national currency in compensation, with the court of final appeal ruling police had arrested her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime here.

But the repeal is incomplete in practice: the same organisation reports transgender people "continue to face threats and harassment," and in December 2022 security forces carried out mass deportations of LGBT people under "security" measures. For a trans traveler: no criminal exposure for gender expression itself, courts now provide recourse, but police harassment and deportation risk remain real.
blindOutOfScope: Migrant-worker labour conditions affect all foreign workers; only trans-specific risk to visitors is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: An academic's overview essay (2016) on transgender issues in this part of the world: gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable; notes a major international film about a transgender pioneer was banned by censors here, among other countries; discusses cross-dressing as a crime across the region.

An international human-rights organisation (Jan 2008): this country's penal-code provision criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex' invites arbitrary arrest and abuse of gender-nonconforming people.
The same organisation (Feb 2022): this country's constitutional court strikes down the provision criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex'.

NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying entry in a foreign legislature's legal-research database covers the same constitutional-court ruling striking down the 2007 provision.

A foreign government's 2023 human-rights country report on this country: significant issues include laws criminalising consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults 'which were enforced', torture reports, arbitrary detention, restrictions on expression and assembly, and extensive gender-based violence.

International human-rights organisation's 2024 world report, chapter on this country: authorities used penal code, national security and cybercrime laws to restrict speech; includes a sexual-orientation and gender-identity section; notes gender-segregation decisions at the national university.

Regional rights monitor (July 2024): analysis of steps forward after the abolition of the 2007 provision - the amendment criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex in any way' (introduced by a religious-conservative MP) was struck down by the constitutional court in 2022; the article traces the law's origins and impact on gender-nonconforming people.

Trans-rights advocacy organisation's reporting: transgender discrimination continues in this country despite the court ruling - enforcement and social discrimination persist after the 2007 provision was struck down.

International human-rights organisation report (April 2018) on LGBT activism across the region - includes this country's criminalisation and an annex of laws used regionwide to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression.
blindTangential: Same-sex conduct remains criminalised at up to 7 years — a situational risk for trans visitors with partners.
